newsitem.title: TURKEY: U.S. backs off wheat subsidy battle, for now.
newsitem.headline: U.S. backs off wheat subsidy battle, for now.

text.p: The United States is backing off a subsidy battle with the European Union over wheat exports but may not do so for long if world prices continue to suffer, grain traders said on Wednesday.

Competition is growing fierce between exporters now that bumper crops in much of the world have cut wheat prices by as much as half from records set just five months ago, said traders at an industry gathering in southern Turkey.
"Things are going to be pretty rough in the next few months, especially when crops start arriving in Australia and Argentina (in December)," a senior grain executive predicted.

The U.S. and Europe, two major exporters who traditionally use subsidies to shore up grain exports, suspended the aid last year as supplies tightened after a series of poor harvests that sent world grain stocks to 20-year lows.
But pressure is growing on Washington to revert to export subsidies after the EU restored its own programme last week to shield its farmers from the new fall in world prices.
The U.S. grain industry has already applied for help with exports of wheat flour, traders said.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said on Tuesday he had not ruled out restoring Washington's so-called Export Enhancement Programme (EEP) but it was too early to do so yet.
EU farm director-general Guy Legras also sounded conciliatory in comments made on Wednesday.

"Subsidies are destined to bring European prices in line with world prices and allow normal exports without any intention to cut prices or to be aggressive," he said. Benchmark wheat prices paid by importers have dropped to around $160 per tonne after almost $300 last year, traders said.
Without subsidies, European wheat is worth closer to $180 per tonne while unsubsidised Argentine wheat is being promised ahead of harvest for as little as $140.
"People are buying hand-to-mouth at the moment. They are all waiting to see if prices keep going down," another trader said.
If export subsidies are used in the coming year, it will be a long-awaited first test of the Uruguay Round global trade pact on agriculture which came into force last year, restricting aid.
The pact commits the U.S. and Europe to reducing subsidised exports by 21 percent over six years to 2001. But it gathered dust for 12 months when subsidies unexpectedly disappeared.

Analysts and even some of the agreement's negotiators believe it may still lack teeth, because last year's unused quotas of some 20 million tonnes of subsidised sales by each side can technically be added to this year's allocations.
That would notionally set a ceiling far higher than either side's ability to export and leave room for a grain trade war. They must, however, reach the final targets on time in 2001.
But while traders expect aggressive competition, few believe either Brussels or Washington is ready to return to a full-scale subsidy feud that ate up billions of dollars during the 1980s.
A U.S. official told the conference in Turkey that Washington had been in touch with the European Commission in Brussels to try to steer it away from using subsidies.
The EU appears to have ignored the advice, but modest initial aid worth less than $2 million suggests a soft-pedal approach, traders said.
"I don't think the Americans want to use EEP this year but it depends on what happens in the market. They won't stand back and see their market share fall to pieces," one trader said.
